analysis.one_liner: Takes congressional map-drawing away from legislators and gives it to independent citizen commissions.
analysis.headline: Backed by 84 House Democrats, the Redistricting Reform Act of 2019 sat in a House Judiciary subcommittee for a year and a half and never received a committee or floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every state to draw its congressional districts with an independent commission of ordinary citizens rather than elected legislators, using citizens screened for conflicts of interest, with public hearings, posted maps and data, and a ban on drawing maps to favor any political party. It also would have banned mid-decade redistricting, a practice used to redraw maps for partisan advantage between censuses. If a state's commission process broke down, a three-judge federal court would draw the plan instead. The federal government would have paid states $150,000 for each congressional seat to run the commissions. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee in June 2019 and to its Constitution subcommittee a month later, and never moved again [S2] [S3] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters in states where legislators currently draw the maps. Commissioners would be randomly selected citizens barred from serving if they, or their immediate family, held office, ran campaigns, lobbied, or worked for elected officials during a ten-year window [S3]. Commissions would have to hold public hearings, post draft and final maps with the underlying data and mapping software online, and accept public comments and citizen-submitted maps [S3]. Districts could not unduly favor any political party, and states could not redraw maps between censuses except when a court requires it [S3]. Incumbent members of Congress would no longer be able to shape the districts they run in.

how_it_helps.text: Maps would be drawn by a 15-member citizen commission whose members are screened out if they or immediate family members held office, worked in campaigns, or lobbied during covered periods, and whose approval rules require cross-party support for any final plan.

The commission could not consider where a member of Congress lives or the party affiliation or voting history of a district's population, and plans could not unduly favor or disfavor any political party statewide.

The commission would have to hold at least six public hearings, stream its meetings, post all draft and final maps, the underlying data, and the mapping software online, and accept maps submitted by any member of the public.

States that redistrict under the Act could not be redistricted again until after the next decennial census, unless a court requires it, closing the door on mid-decade map redraws for partisan advantage.
The Attorney General or any aggrieved state citizen could sue to enforce the law, with cases heard by a three-judge court and appealed directly to the Supreme Court.

analysis.who_pays: State legislators and the two major parties lose the power to draw congressional maps, which is the point of the bill. Members of Congress would lose a tool that protects their own seats. Federal taxpayers would fund the commissions through payments of $150,000 per congressional seat, and the small number of citizens who serve as commissioners and staff would take on the work. In the rare case where a commission fails, unelected federal judges would draw the map.
analysis.who_pays_short: Legislators, party officials, and federal taxpayers

drawbacks.text: If a state fails to establish a commission or the commission cannot agree on a plan, a three-judge federal court draws the map instead, meaning unelected judges, possibly advised by a special master, could end up deciding districts in states where the citizen process breaks down.

The bill overrides state legislative authority over redistricting, based on Congress's constitutional power over the 'time, place, and manner' of House elections, a use of federal power that raises questions about Washington dictating how states run their own elections.

Commission members are barred from donating more than $1,000 to campaigns, holding office, or working for campaigns or lobbyists for roughly a decade around their service, a disqualification regime so broad that critics argue it screens out experienced and civically engaged people.
Federal payments of $150,000 per congressional seat, funded by taxpayers, would cover the cost of running the commissions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — taking map-drawing away from the people whose seats the maps protect — is substantial, and the bill's transparency, cross-party approval, and enforcement provisions are more detailed than most anti-gerrymandering proposals. The serious costs are real but narrower: a court backstop that hands map-drawing to federal judges when commissions fail, a hard-to-defend federal override of state processes, a disqualification screen that may exclude engaged citizens, and a taxpayer-funded price tag. The transparency requirements and judicial enforcement temper the risk that commissions become opaque or captured.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its Constitution subcommittee in July 2019, and sat there with no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote through the end of the Congress in January 2021 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Zoe Lofgren introduced the bill on June 27, 2019, joined by 35 other initial cosponsors, all of them California Democrats.
The House referred the bill to the Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and on July 30, 2019 referred it to the Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties.
A total of 83 members cosponsored the bill, all Democrats; no Republican cosponsored it.
No further action was taken on the bill for the remainder of the 116th Congress, which ended January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of Congress and state legislators of both parties, who kept the power to draw the congressional maps that shape their own reelections. Because the bill died without a vote, no state had to give up legislative control of map-drawing under its terms.

for.name: Rep. Zoe Lofgren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Redistricting Reform Act of 2019 and recruited cosponsors.

for.name: 83 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.

against.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
against.what_they_did: The committee received the bill the day it was introduced and referred it to a subcommittee; no markup or committee vote was ever scheduled, and the bill never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 84 members who sponsored or cosponsored the bill were Democrats, including all 36 initial cosponsors from California; no Republican signed on and the bill never reached a vote, so the full partisan split was never measured [S3] [S4].

industries.industry: Incumbent officeholders and the two major parties
industries.note: The bill removes map-drawing from the legislators and party officials whose seats the maps protect, and bans plans that favor either party statewide. For them the bill is a direct loss of power over their own reelections, so their interest runs against voters who want competitive, fairly drawn districts.

Partisan map consultants lose their legislative clients, since legislators would no longer draw maps. Commission vendors would still be hired, but under public application, disclosure of a decade of political spending, and disqualification rules for those with campaign ties.
